docs.title: Environment Variable Migration
docs.text:
The following env vars have been replaced by settings. If detected at startup, they are automatically migrated to the settings database and a deprecation warning is logged.

Old Env Var New Setting Notes STASH_RATE_LIMIT stash_api_rate ENABLE_BODY_SIGNAL body_signal_enabled ENABLE_TATTOO_SIGNAL tattoo_signal_enabled FACE_CANDIDATES face_candidates

Env vars that remain (connection strings and secrets): - STASH_URL, STASH_API_KEY, DATA_DIR, LOG_LEVEL - Per-endpoint *_URL and *_API_KEY vars

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text: File Purpose api/hardware.py Hardware detection, tier classification api/settings.py Setting definitions, tier defaults, resolution logic, env var migration api/settings_router.py FastAPI endpoints for settings and system info

docs.title: Startup Sequence
docs.text:
1. init_hardware(data_dir) — probes hardware, classifies tier
  2. init_settings(db, tier) — creates settings manager with tier defaults
  3. migrate_env_vars(mgr) — one-time migration of deprecated env vars
  4. Sidecar logs hardware summary and active tier

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Settings overrides are stored in the user_settings table of stash_sense.db with a settings. key prefix. The table uses a simple key-value structure with JSON-encoded values.

docs.title: Stash-Box Endpoints
docs.text:
Note: Database building has moved to the stash-sense-trainer repository. This document is preserved for reference but the build commands below apply to the trainer repo.

This document describes the different stash-box endpoints supported for building face recognition databases, their characteristics, and considerations for each.

docs.title: Supported Endpoints
docs.text: Endpoint API Type Performers Images/Performer Rate Limit StashDB GraphQL ~100,000+ Multiple 240/min safe ThePornDB REST ~10,000 Multiple 240/min safe PMVStash GraphQL ~6,500 3.7 avg 300/min+ JAVStash GraphQL ~21,700 1.0 avg 300/min+ FansDB GraphQL Unknown Unknown Untested

docs.title: StashDB (Primary)
docs.text:
• URL: https://stashdb.org/graphql
  • API: Standard stash-box GraphQL
  • Use: database_builder.py directly
  • Notes: Largest database, highest quality metadata

docs.title: ThePornDB
docs.text:
• URL: https://api.theporndb.net (REST API)
  • API: REST, NOT GraphQL (despite Stash config showing /graphql)
  • Use: build_theporndb.py (custom script)
  • Notes:
  • Has pre-cropped face thumbnails (face_url field)
  • Many performers cross-reference StashDB IDs
  • Rate limit ~275/min, safe at 240/min

docs.title: PMVStash
docs.text:
• URL: https://pmvstash.org/graphql
  • API: Standard stash-box GraphQL
  • Use: database_builder.py with env override
  • Notes:
  • PMV-focused content
  • Good image coverage (100% have images)
  • 34% have multiple images (avg 3.7)
  • Portrait images (1280x1920)

docs.title: JAVStash
docs.text:
• URL: https://javstash.org/graphql
  • API: Standard stash-box GraphQL
  • Use: database_builder.py with env override
  • Notes:
  • JAV-focused content with Japanese names
  • Limited to ~1 image per performer (see below)
  • Square images (705x705)

docs.title: Database Building
docs.text: Database building is handled by a separate private training pipeline. Pre-built databases are published as releases on the stash-sense-data repository.

docs.title: JAVStash: Single Image Limitation
docs.text: Problem: JAVStash performers typically have only 1 image, which limits face recognition accuracy. Our standard approach of building multiple embeddings per performer (target: 5) doesn't work here.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• Single embedding = higher false positive/negative rates
  • No redundancy for poor-quality source images
  • Can't leverage voting across multiple embeddings

docs.title: Potential Solutions (TODO: Discuss)
docs.text:
1. Scene Frame Extraction
  2. JAVStash has scene data with fingerprints
  3. Could extract frames from matched scenes in user's library
  4. Build embeddings from actual video content

  5. Requires: scene matching pipeline, user's local content

  6. External Image Sources

  7. Cross-reference with other databases (e.g., JAV actress databases)
  8. Scrape additional images from linked URLs in performer metadata

  9. Ethical/legal considerations for scraping

  10. Data Augmentation

  11. Generate synthetic variations of single image
  12. Horizontal flip, slight rotations, color adjustments

  13. Risk: may not improve real-world accuracy

  14. Lower Confidence Threshold

  15. Accept that JAV matching will be lower confidence
  16. Use separate threshold for JAV vs other sources

  17. Let users decide on match acceptance

  18. Ensemble with ThePornDB

  19. Some JAV content exists on ThePornDB
  20. Cross-reference and merge embeddings where possible

  21. ThePornDB has StashDB links that might map to JAVStash

  22. User-Contributed Images

  23. Allow users to contribute additional performer images
  24. Build community-sourced image database
  25. Privacy/consent considerations

docs.title: Recommended Approach
docs.text:
Short-term: Options 1 (scene frames) and 4 (adjusted thresholds): - Don't require external data sources - Leverage data users already have - Can be implemented incrementally

Long-term: Option 7 - Crowd-Sourced Cloud Service

The ultimate solution is a public cloud service (similar to stash-box) where users can submit face embeddings extracted from their identified scenes. This would: - Bypass the single-image limitation entirely - Build models from real scene content, not just promo images - Scale with the community (more users = better models) - Preserve privacy (only embeddings, never raw images)

docs.title: Rate Limit Reference
docs.text:
Tested January 2026:

Endpoint Tested Rate Result StashDB 240/min ✅ No issues (running 24h+) ThePornDB 240/min ✅ Safe (limit ~275/min) ThePornDB 360/min ❌ 429s at ~275 requests PMVStash 300/min ✅ No issues JAVStash 300/min ✅ No issues (slower response)

Recommendation: Use 240/min (0.25s delay) for all endpoints as a safe default.

docs.title: Container won't start
docs.text:
Check logs: 

docker logs stash-sense

Common causes:

  • Missing database files - ensure /data contains the .voy files
  • GPU driver issues - try without GPU first to isolate
  • Port conflict - change from 6960 to another port

docs.title: "Database not loaded"
docs.text:
The face recognition database hasn't been downloaded yet. This is normal on first startup.

Fix: Navigate to /plugins/stash-sense in Stash, go to the Settings tab, and click Update in the Database section to download the database.

Alternatively, verify the volume mount has database files:

docker exec stash-sense ls -la /data

Should show face_facenet.voy, face_arcface.voy, performers.json, manifest.json. If empty, either download via the Settings UI or check your volume mount path.

docs.title: "Load model from /app/models/facenet512.onnx failed: File doesn't exist"
docs.text:
The ONNX face recognition models are not bundled in the Docker image — they need to be downloaded after first startup.

Fix: Navigate to /plugins/stash-sense in Stash, go to the Settings tab, and click Download All in the Models section. This downloads FaceNet512 (~90 MB) and ArcFace (~130 MB) to /data/models/.

Alternatively, download via the API:

curl -X POST http://localhost:6960/models/download-all

docs.title: Health check shows "degraded"
docs.text: This is expected on first startup before the database and models are downloaded. Once you download both from the Settings tab, the status will change to "healthy" after the first identification request.

docs.title: Health check failing
docs.text:
# Test manually
curl http://localhost:6960/health

# Check container status
docker ps -a | grep stash-sense

If container is restarting, check logs for the error.

docs.title: "CUDA not available"
docs.text:
The container fell back to CPU mode.

Verify GPU is accessible: 

docker exec stash-sense nvidia-smi

If this fails:

  1. Ensure nvidia-container-toolkit is installed
  2. Container needs --runtime=nvidia --gpus all
  3. Restart Docker daemon after toolkit install

docs.title: "CUDA out of memory"
docs.text:
GPU memory exhausted. Check what's using it:

nvidia-smi

Solutions: - Stop other GPU-using containers temporarily - Use CPU mode (slower but works)

docs.title: Slow performance on GPU
docs.text:
If GPU is detected but still slow:

  1. Check GPU utilization during requests: watch nvidia-smi
  2. Ensure models aren't being re-downloaded (mount model cache volume)
  3. First request is slow (model loading) - subsequent requests should be faster

docs.title: Plugin can't reach sidecar
docs.text:
From Stash container, test connectivity: 

docker exec stash curl http://stash-sense-host:6960/health

Common fixes:

  • Use host IP if containers are on different Docker networks
  • Check firewall isn't blocking port 6960
  • Verify the Sidecar URL in plugin settings matches your container's host and port

docs.title: Sidecar can't reach Stash
docs.text:
Test from sidecar: 

docker exec stash-sense curl http://your-stash-host:9999/graphql

Common fixes:

  • Verify STASH_URL environment variable is correct
  • Verify STASH_API_KEY is valid
  • Check Stash is running and accessible
  • Don't use localhost in STASH_URL — it refers to the container itself, not the host. Use the host's LAN IP.

docs.title: Windows: "Connection refused" on localhost
docs.text:
On recent Docker Desktop versions, localhost may resolve to ::1 (IPv6) instead of 127.0.0.1. Try:

  • Use http://127.0.0.1:6960 instead of http://localhost:6960
  • Use the machine's LAN IP (e.g., http://192.168.1.100:6960)

See the Windows / WSL section of the installation guide for more details.

docs.title: Plugin Python dependencies
docs.text:
The plugin backend requires the requests library in Stash's Python environment.

Symptoms: Plugin appears installed but all sidecar requests fail silently. Stash logs may show ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'.

Fix: Install requests in Stash's Python environment:

# If Stash runs in Docker:
docker exec stash pip install requests

# If Stash runs natively:
pip install requests

docs.title: Plugin backend not working
docs.text:
Check Stash logs for Python errors:

docker logs stash 2>&1 | grep -i "stash.sense\|error\|traceback"

Common causes:

  • Plugin files not installed correctly — reinstall from the plugin source
  • Python not available in Stash's environment
  • Sidecar URL not configured in plugin settings

docs.title: Plugin not appearing
docs.text:
1. Check plugin files are in the correct location
  2. Reload plugins in Stash settings
  3. Check Stash logs for errors

docs.title: Credentials not detected
docs.text:
The sidecar reads Stash-Box endpoint credentials from Stash's Settings > Metadata Providers at startup. If endpoints aren't showing up:

  1. Verify the endpoint is configured in Stash's Metadata Providers
  2. Restart the sidecar, or use the Refresh button in the plugin's Settings tab
  3. Check sidecar logs for errors during endpoint discovery

docs.title: Endpoint not available for upstream sync
docs.text: Make sure the endpoint is enabled in the plugin's Settings tab. Disabled endpoints are skipped during analysis but their configuration is preserved.

docs.title: No faces detected
docs.text:
• No sprite sheets: Generate sprite sheets first (Settings > Tasks > Generate > Sprites)
  • Low quality sprites: Regenerate with higher quality settings
  • No clear face shots: Some scenes don't have good face visibility
  • Very small faces: Detection has a minimum size threshold

docs.title: Wrong matches
docs.text:
• High distance score: Scores above 0.5 are less reliable
  • Similar looking performers: Some faces are genuinely similar
  • Database coverage: The performer may not be in the database or may have poor reference images

docs.title: Performer matched but not in library
docs.text:
This is expected — the face matched a performer in the database who you haven't added to your Stash yet. Options:

  1. Click "View on Stash-Box" to verify the match
  2. Add the performer to your Stash manually
  3. Use Stash's "Identify" feature to import from a Stash-Box endpoint

docs.title: Corrupt database files
docs.text:
If you see index errors or crashes on load:

# Remove and re-download via Settings UI, or manually:
rm -rf /path/to/data/*.voy /path/to/data/performers.db /path/to/data/*.json
# Then download fresh via Settings tab > Database > Update

docs.title: Outdated database
docs.text:
Check current version: 

curl http://localhost:6960/database/info

Compare with the latest release on GitHub. New databases include more performers and improved embeddings.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you're stuck:

  1. Check container logs: docker logs stash-sense
  2. Test health endpoint: curl http://localhost:6960/health
  3. Verify database files exist and have correct permissions
  4. Open an issue on GitHub with:
  5. Container logs
  6. Health endpoint response
  7. Docker/Unraid version
  8. GPU model (if applicable)

docs.title: Content Index
docs.text:
Unfinished feature: the job is hidden until Settings > Features > Show Unfinished Features is on. It becomes visible when duplicate detection (#130) ships. That job reads this index, so run Content Index first.

The content index answers one question for the whole library: does the content of one file appear inside another, and where? Stash's perceptual hash can't answer it. A trimmed intro, letterboxing or a watermark moves every frame it samples, and a clip inside a longer file never matches. Duplicate detection, split detection and the quality flags build on this index.

docs.title: What it stores
docs.text:
For every file, once per content (the same bytes in two places count once):

  • An audio fingerprint: Chromaprint over the whole soundtrack, about 8 values a second. It finds a clip inside a longer file and gives the offset to a fraction of a second.
  • A video signature: a 64-bit hash of every keyframe, with its time. It catches what audio can't: the same picture with another soundtrack, such as a dubbed version or a re-scored edit.
  • Overlaps: for each pair of files sharing audio, which stretch of one file is which stretch of the other, and how closely they match.

Everything lives in content_fp.db in the data directory (about 1.8 GB for 28,000 files), apart from stash_sense.db. The lookup index (content_index/, about 1.3 GB) sits beside it and is rebuilt when files are added.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Run Content Index from Operations, or schedule it there. Each run:

  1. Reads the exclusion list (see Curation Settings). A file is skipped when any of its scenes is excluded. If Stash can't be reached, the run stops.
  2. Fingerprints every file that has no fingerprint yet. A run with up to 200 files to do takes the most recently added scenes first. A larger backlog, such as the first pass over a library, is taken in a scattered order so that parallel workers read from different disks.
  3. Rebuilds the lookup index if files were added, then looks up each new file and records its overlaps.

The job is safe to stop or restart. A finished file is never fingerprinted again, so a stopped run carries on where it left off. It also gives way to higher-priority CPU work.

It reads files through the media mount (see Configuration). If 50 files in a row are missing, the run stops with a message to check MEDIA_PATH_MAP and the /media mount, so a bad mount doesn't make it skip the whole library.

docs.title: CPU use
docs.text:
ffmpeg runs under the Media Job Priority (nice) and Media Job Threads settings in Settings > Performance. Content Index Workers (default 2) sets how many files are processed at once. Each file costs about one decode of its audio plus its keyframes, a few seconds of CPU for a 30-minute scene, so the first pass over a large library is limited by disk reads, not CPU: each ffmpeg uses about a tenth of one core.

On an array of spinning disks (unRAID), each worker keeps one disk busy while it reads a file. Playback from a disk the job is reading can stutter; other disks are unaffected. Two workers on the same disk seek against each other and read slower than one, which is why a large backlog is taken in scattered order. More workers finish the first pass sooner but keep more disks busy at once.

docs.title: Importing a store built elsewhere
docs.text:
A store built by the standalone worker (python -m content_fingerprint.cli) on another machine can be imported instead of fingerprinting those files again:

  1. Stop the worker that built it, so its last writes are in the main file (or copy the -wal file alongside, renamed to match), then copy it into the data directory as content_fp_import.db (on unRAID: /mnt/nvme_cache/appdata/stash-sense/data/).
  2. Run Content Index.

Before copying anything, the job fingerprints a sample of the imported files itself (a few of each file type) and compares the results byte for byte. Fingerprints depend on the ffmpeg build: ffmpeg 4.4 and 6.1 agree on AAC and MP3 audio but not on WMA, for example. If any sample differs, nothing is imported, the file is renamed to content_fp_import.db.refused, and the run's result says which file types differed and which ffmpeg builds were involved. The job then fingerprints those files itself. After a successful import, the file is renamed to content_fp_import.db.imported and can be deleted.

Only files still in the library are imported. Video signatures and overlaps are not imported; the job computes them.

docs.title: How matches are judged
docs.text:
Audio overlaps are kept when a stretch of at least 20 seconds matches with a bit error rate of 0.25 or less. Measured on a real library:

Bit error rate Meaning 0.04-0.2 The same content (a re-encode, a remux, a re-release) 0.3-0.4 Grey zone: often different scenes of one production sharing a music bed 0.45 and up Unrelated

A pair of files sharing audio is classed by how much of each file the overlap covers: duplicate (most of both), contained (most of the shorter file sits inside the longer one, like a scene inside a DVD rip), partial (a long unbroken shared stretch) or incidental (short scraps, such as an intro sting or a music bed).

Video signatures are compared pair by pair, by the consumer that needs them. A match reports the time offset and the share of comparable keyframes that match. Only keyframes, not every frame, are decoded, which costs about 40 times less. Two encodes rarely put keyframes at the same moments, though, so only some keyframes can be compared. Measured on real files: duplicates at 0.25-1.0, different scenes from the same studio at 0.03 or less, and unrelated files share no matching keyframes at all.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A file without an audio track has no audio fingerprint; its video signature still works.
  • One pair in sixteen real duplicates tested (an AVI against an MP4 re-render) gave a video offset 10 seconds away from the audio's. Prefer the audio offset when both exist.
  • Overlaps already recorded stay in the store when a scene is later excluded; features reading them filter by the exclusion list.

docs.title: Curation Settings
docs.text:
Two settings apply to every Stash Sense curation feature: an exclusion list of content nothing may touch, and the video formats you would rather not keep. Both are stored in Stash itself, so other tools can read them too.

Edit them in Stash Sense > Settings > Curation.

docs.title: Never touch (exclusion list)
docs.text:
Pick tags, groups and studios. Ids that are not numbers are ignored. A scene matching any of them is excluded:

  • A tag excludes scenes with that tag or any of its child tags, at any depth.
  • A group excludes scenes in that group or any of its sub-groups.
  • A studio excludes scenes from that studio or any of its child studios, so a network covers all its sites.

For an excluded scene, Stash Sense:

  • never fingerprints it (face fingerprints are skipped);
  • never creates a recommendation for it, and hides any existing recommendation that names it, including a duplicate pair where only one scene is excluded;
  • refuses any action on it: preview, accept, batch accept, revert, merge, delete, update, and scene identification. The refusal names the scene and points here.

Changes apply immediately after Save. Every write action and every analysis run reads the list fresh from Stash; the dashboard's lists refresh within a minute. When you take something off the list, the next run of each analysis checks its scenes again in full.

Stash Sense also never sends an excluded scene's fingerprints to a stash-box when looking for matches.

If Stash can't be reached, analysis runs and write actions are refused rather than risk touching an excluded scene. The dashboard keeps showing lists filtered by the last exclusion list it read.

Merging performers is refused when a performer being merged away appears in an excluded scene, because the merge rewrites the performers on those scenes.

docs.title: Disfavored formats
docs.text:
Two comma-separated lists: video codecs as Stash reports them (for example hevc, av1, vp9) and containers (for example wmv, avi).

They are taste, not quality. When Stash Sense suggests which of a scene's files to keep, a better file still wins on resolution and bitrate. A disfavored format only decides between files that are otherwise equal. With both lists empty, no codec or container is preferred.

docs.title: Reading the settings from other tools
docs.text:
The settings live in the stash-sense plugin's configuration in Stash. Any tool with a Stash API key can read them:

query { configuration { plugins } }

plugins["stash-sense"] holds these curation keys, empty by default unless noted:

Key Contents excludeTagIds Tag ids excludeGroupIds Group ids excludeStudioIds Studio ids disfavoredVideoCodecs Lowercase codec names disfavoredContainers Lowercase container names qualityReportOnly Boolean, on by default: quality flag cards record answers and change nothing qualityGroupBroken, qualityGroupRip, qualityGroupBelowStudio, qualityGroupFormat One group id each: the work-queue group an accepted quality card adds the scene to qualityPeerPercentile Number from 1 to 50, default 10: the below-studio percentile

To resolve the exclusion list to scenes, query findScenes with each list as a tags, groups or studios criterion, using modifier: INCLUDES and depth: -1, and take the union.

Writing the settings

Stash's configurePlugin mutation replaces the plugin's entire settings map. Read the current map, change your keys, then write the whole map back. Sending only your keys erases the others, including the sidecar URL.

The same fields also appear under Stash's Settings > Plugins > Stash Sense as plain text.

docs.title: Duplicate Detection
docs.text:
Hidden as unfinished

Duplicate Scenes is hidden until it passes the production-ready checklist. It replaces the legacy Duplicate Scenes (legacy) and Duplicate Scene Files (legacy) types (#130), which are hidden too. To use it now, turn on Settings > Features > Show Unfinished Features and reload the page. Existing recommendations are kept and reappear when the setting is on.

Stash Sense finds copies of the same scene that Stash's phash matching misses, and helps you merge them and keep the best file. For each set of duplicates you see a review card. It shows both scenes, the file Stash Sense would keep and why, and stills from the matching moments. Nothing changes until you accept.

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text:
Phash compares a few frames. A trimmed intro, black bars, a re-encode, an upscale or a watermark moves them, and a scene inside a longer file never matches. Duplicate detection compares the sound and the picture instead, so it finds:

  • trims and different intros or outros
  • letterboxed, cropped or watermarked copies
  • re-encodes and upscales
  • a scene that sits inside a longer file, such as a DVD rip
  • the same scene with another soundtrack, such as a dub

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• The Content Index job, for the best results. Run it first. It has already fingerprinted the audio and keyframes of your files, so this job reads them from the index instead of decoding the files again. Without the index, the job fingerprints the audio of each file it checks, which is slower.
  • Sprites in Stash. Stash's generated sprite sheets give the job a way to compare pictures. Generate them for your scenes in Stash (Settings > Tasks > Generate). A scene without a sprite sheet is still checked by audio and keyframes.
  • The media mount, so the job can read the files. See Configuration.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Run Duplicate Scenes from Operations, or schedule it there. The job:

  1. Reads the exclusion list (see Curation Settings). If Stash can't be reached, the run stops.
  2. Finds candidate pairs.
  3. Checks each pair against the evidence.
  4. Groups the pairs that hold up into sets and writes one recommendation per set.
  5. Health checks the file it would keep in each set that would delete anything.

Then open the dashboard and look for the Duplicate Scenes tile. Each card is one set. See Reviewing Recommendations for how cards work.

docs.title: How candidates are found and checked
docs.text:
Comparing every scene with every other would take too long. The job first collects pairs from cheap sources:

  • the same Stash-Box ID
  • the same studio and title
  • the same studio, date and performers
  • a close phash
  • a shared URL
  • two files in one scene
  • an overlap the Content Index found in the audio

Each pair is then checked, in this order:

  1. Audio fingerprint. The job compares the soundtracks. A low error rate means the same recording, and it also gives the offset between the two files.
  2. Keyframes. The job compares the stored keyframe signatures of both files. This catches the same picture with a different soundtrack.
  3. Sprite tiles. The job compares the tiles of the two sprite sheets. It only does this when audio and keyframes can't settle the pair. Tiles that recur across many scenes of a studio, such as logos and intro cards, are ignored.

A match on sprites is good evidence. A miss proves nothing. Sprites sample only 81 moments, and a trimmed copy lands on different ones. So a pair with no sprite match is never called different on that alone.

A pair that shows no evidence at all, because none of the three could be computed, is dropped. There is nothing for you to judge.

docs.title: The classes
docs.text:
Every card has a class. The class decides what the card offers and what accept does.

Class What it means What the card offers Duplicate The same content in both scenes. Merge the scenes, keep the best file, delete the rest. You can pick another file, or a second file to keep. Contained One scene sits inside a longer file. The longer file is never deleted. See Contained cards. Partial A long stretch is shared, but each side has more. Nothing changes. Accept only marks it resolved. Language variant The same picture with another soundtrack. Merge the scenes and keep every file. Mislabel The files match, but the metadata disagrees: different Stash-Box IDs, studios, or no performer in common. Choose which scene has the right metadata. The scenes merge into it. Review The evidence is unclear. Nothing changes. Look at the pair, then resolve it.

A shared music bed or an intro sting is not enough for any class. Pairs that share only that are left out.

docs.title: How the keeper is chosen
docs.text:
The card suggests one file to keep and says why in a sentence. The rules run in this order, and the first one that separates the files decides:

  1. A rip loses to a clean file. (Rips are not flagged yet, so this rule rarely fires.)
  2. An AI upscale loses to its original.
  3. The file with more real detail wins. This weighs the pixels against the bit rate, and counts hevc and av1 as more efficient than h264.
  4. A codec or container you disfavored loses, but only when the detail is about equal.
  5. More bits per pixel wins, since that is a cleaner picture with fewer blocks.
  6. A clearly higher frame rate wins.
  7. For duplicates, a file more than a minute longer wins, since it is more complete.
  8. A better container (mp4, m4v, mkv) wins.

If nothing separates the files, the card says they are practically equal and keeps one. Either is fine.

A few cases keep two files:

  • An upscale pair. If a set holds both an original and an upscale, Stash Sense keeps the best of each and deletes the other copies.
  • A longer file that is worse. If the best file is much shorter than another copy, the longest file is kept too, because it may hold extra content, such as a supercut. You decide.
  • A contained scene that is better. If the short file is strictly better quality than the longer cut that holds it, both stay. See Contained cards.

An AI upscale is detected from the file name, the folder, the encoder tag, or an av1 file much larger in pixels or size than its siblings. hevc and vp9 files are never flagged by size alone, since real HD releases use them.

The disfavored codecs and containers come from the exclusion and format settings in Curation Settings. They only break near ties. They never override a clear difference in quality.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: Before a card offers to delete anything, the job probes the file it would keep and decodes a few short windows spread through it. A truncated or damaged file fails. A file that fails is never the keeper while a healthy one exists. If no file in the set passes, the card keeps every file and deletes nothing.

docs.title: How well it agrees with you
docs.text: On the owner's library, the suggestion matched the recorded pick in 92.8% of 567 scored pairs. Practical ties and contained pairs deferred to splitting are left out. The pairs and every disagreement are listed in the keeper regression.

docs.title: What accept does
docs.text:
Accept runs the outcome the card shows, in this order:

  1. Merge the scenes in Stash. The scene with the most history stays. Scenes with a play count, an O count, a rating, the organized flag or groups rank first. Empty fields on it are filled from the others. Performers, tags, URLs, groups and galleries are unioned. Play and O history moves to the scene that stays.
  2. Delete the files not kept. A confirm names each file by path and size first. If Stash has a trash folder (Settings > System > Trash path), the files go there. If not, they are permanently deleted.

If a scene changed after the card loaded, accept is refused and the card reloads. Every accept is logged, and metadata can be reverted from the apply log. Deleted files cannot be brought back.

docs.title: Contained cards
docs.text:
Quality decides, and the workflow is always merge first (to collect the metadata), then delete the lower-quality file. The longer file is never deleted.

  • The longer file holds several scenes (it is at least 1.5 times as long as the shorter file). The card says to split the longer file first and changes nothing: no merge and no delete. This keeps a scene from being merged into an unsplit multi-scene file. Split detection is meant to run before duplicate detection; until the longer file is split, these cards leave both files alone.
  • A re-cut where the shorter file is strictly better. Both files stay and the scenes stay separate.
  • A re-cut at equal quality, or where the longer cut is better. At equal quality the longer, more complete cut is kept. The shorter scene merges into the longer cut's scene, whatever history either has: the longer scene's values win, empty fields are filled from the shorter scene, and performers, tags, URLs, groups and galleries are unioned. Then the shorter file is deleted.

If you pick another option on the card, it is honored: choosing to keep only the longer file deletes the shorter file and merges its scene into the longer one. Contained cards are never in the batch accept.

docs.title: Mislabel cards
docs.text: A mislabel card never unions metadata. The scene you pick as having the right metadata keeps its fields exactly as they are, and nothing is copied in from the other scene.

docs.title: Your pick is remembered
docs.text: Files are picked by file hash, not by position on the card. If you keep a different file than the suggestion, the choice and the evidence are saved as a labeled example, and it means the same file however the card is ordered.

docs.title: Accept all high-confidence
docs.text:
Batch accept is limited to the plain case. A card qualifies only when all of these hold:

  • the class is duplicate
  • you have not changed the suggestion
  • exactly one file is kept, and at least one is deleted
  • the keeper raised no flag
  • every deleted file is identical to the kept file (same md5 or oshash) or is the same encode (same codec and frame size, duration within a second)

Everything else is left for you to review one card at a time. See Accept all high-confidence.

docs.title: Exclusions
docs.text: The exclusion list is honored. A scene on it is never a candidate, and an existing card that names an excluded scene is hidden. If Stash can't be reached to read the list, the run stops instead of guessing.

docs.title: Cards update in place
docs.text:
Each set has one recommendation. When you run the job again:

  • A set whose evidence or keeper suggestion changed is rewritten in place.
  • A set that gains a scene stays one card.
  • A set that is no longer found is marked stale, but only when the run finished.
  • A card you resolved returns if its details change.
  • A card you dismissed stays dismissed.

Tools that read the driver API follow these changes. A card is never deleted, so a tool never misses that a set went away.

docs.title: Performer Identification
docs.text: Stash Sense identifies performers in your scenes and images using face recognition against a database of 108,000+ performers sourced from multiple Stash-Box endpoints.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sprite sheets generated for scenes you want to identify (Stash: Settings > Tasks > Generate > Sprites)
  • Face recognition database downloaded (plugin Settings tab > Database > Update)
  • ONNX models downloaded (plugin Settings tab > Models > Download All)

Without sprite sheets, the sidecar has no frames to analyze. Without the database and models, there's nothing to match against.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Click Identify Performers on any scene page in Stash
  2. The sidecar extracts frames from the scene's sprite sheet (no video decoding required)
  3. Faces are detected using RetinaFace and aligned via 5-point similarity transform
  4. Each face is embedded using two models (FaceNet512 + ArcFace) with flip-averaging for stability
  5. Embeddings are searched against Voyager vector indices containing 366,000+ face references
  6. Results are clustered by person — the same performer appearing across multiple frames is grouped together
  7. Matched performers are shown with confidence scores and one-click tagging

docs.title: Matching Modes
docs.text:
Clustered frequency matching (default) — Groups detected faces by person using cosine distance, then frequency-matches within each cluster. Multi-frame appearances boost confidence — a performer appearing in 30 out of 60 frames is a much stronger signal than a single-frame detection.

Tagged-performer boost — Performers already tagged on the scene receive a small distance bonus (+0.03), reducing false negatives for known cast members.

docs.title: Gallery and Image Identification
docs.text:
Face recognition extends to gallery images, which are typically higher quality and better-framed than video frames.

  • Single image or full gallery identification
  • Results grouped by performer across images with best/average distance
  • Fingerprint caching avoids re-processing on subsequent requests

docs.title: Additional Signals
docs.text:
Face recognition alone is the primary signal. Two optional signals can improve results when faces are unclear or absent:

  • Body proportions — MediaPipe pose estimation extracts shoulder-hip ratio, leg-torso ratio, and arm-span-height ratio. Mismatches apply a penalty multiplier. Enabled via Settings.
  • Tattoo presence — YOLO-based detection. If the query shows tattoos but a candidate has none, a penalty is applied. Matching tattoo locations give a small boost. Requires the optional tattoo detection models.

Fusion: final_score = face_score × body_multiplier × tattoo_multiplier. Missing signals are neutral (1.0 multiplier).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
On a GTX 1080 (8GB VRAM), a typical scene (60 frames) processes in ~5 seconds. The 3-phase batch pipeline (extract → detect → embed+match) processes all faces in bulk rather than one at a time.

CPU mode works but is significantly slower (~2-3 seconds per frame for face detection vs ~200ms with GPU).

docs.title: Understanding Results
docs.text:
Each detected person shows:

  • Face thumbnails — Cropped faces from the scene frames
  • Best match — Top performer match from the database
  • Distance score — Lower is better (cosine distance, 0.0 = perfect match)
  • Appearances — How many frames this person appeared in

Results are split into two groups:

  • Multi-frame detections — Performers appearing in multiple frames (shown prominently)
  • Single-frame detections — One-off detections (in a collapsible section, less reliable)

docs.title: Result Actions
docs.text: Button Action Add to Scene Links the performer to the scene Already tagged on scene Shown instead of "Add to Scene" for performers already tagged View on Stash-Box Opens the performer's page on the source Stash-Box endpoint

docs.title: Quality Flags
docs.text:
Hidden as unfinished

Quality flags are hidden until they pass the production-ready checklist (#133). To use them now, turn on Settings > Features > Show Unfinished Features and reload the page. Existing recommendations are kept and reappear when the setting is on.

Some files in a library are not what you meant to keep: a download that stopped halfway, a copy ripped from a tube site, a version far smaller than the studio's own release, a format you would rather not have. Stash Sense looks at each scene's primary file and raises up to four flags. Each flagged scene gets one review card where you answer yes or no per flag. Nothing changes in Stash until you accept a card, and by default even accepting changes nothing (see report-only).

This is stage 1. It uses what is already in the file and in your library. Reading text off the picture is stage 2 (see what waits for stage 2).

docs.title: The four flags
docs.text:
Flag What it means What to do Broken The file is missing from disk, will not decode, has no video or no audio, has an index that is gone, or is shorter or longer than Stash says. Open the file. If it really is damaged or cut short, replace it. A few files the sidecar can't see are flagged too, so check the mount first. Tube or leak rip The file name or its embedded tags point at a tube site or carry a link. If it is a rip, look for a clean copy. Below the studio's release The file has much less detail than the studio's other scenes from the same years. Look for the studio's own release of the scene. Disfavored format The file's codec or container is on one of your disfavored lists. Re-encode or replace it, if you care.

A scene can carry several flags. Each one is a separate yes or no on the card.

docs.title: Broken: the tiered check
docs.text:
Checking every file in full would take days, so the check has two tiers.

Cheap pass, every file. Three steps, cached by the file's oshash and size so each file is only read again if it changes:

  1. One ffprobe: are there a video and an audio stream, do their durations agree, and does the file's duration match Stash's (a difference over 2% or 5 seconds, whichever is more).
  2. A container index check. It reads the first and last 4 MB, never the whole file, and finds a missing MP4 moov atom, an AVI with no index or an MKV with no cue points. A moov that is merely at the end of the file (no faststart) is only a note, not damage.
  3. A decode of the last 30 seconds, where a cut-short download shows its errors.

The result is ok, warn (small oddities such as a few seconds of trailing audio, or an index that makes seeking slow) or suspect (a hard failure above). Only a suspect continues.

Deep check, suspects only. The same 24-window health check that duplicate detection uses: 24 one-second decodes spread across the file. A window that fails is decoded again from 20 seconds earlier, because a seek artifact vanishes on the second try and real damage repeats. The deep result is final, so a file the cheap pass doubts can still come out clean. Deep results are stored in the Content Index store and shared with duplicate detection, so a file checked by one is not checked again by the other. If you have not built a content index yet, the deep check still runs, but its result is not kept.

A file that is not on disk is flagged broken but is not cached, so it is checked again next run once the mount is back. A check that timed out or could not start is not cached either; the next run tries again. When more than 2% of the checked files (and more than 10) are missing in one run, the job treats it as a media mount problem: it raises no flag for those files, leaves their open cards as they are, and logs a warning.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: The cheap pass reads a few megabytes and decodes 30 seconds per file, two files at a time. On a spinning disk the first run over a large library takes hours, and later runs mostly read the cache. The deep check adds 24 short decodes for each suspect, which is a small fraction of the library. The job runs at low priority and needs the media mount like the other jobs that read files. See Configuration.

docs.title: Below the studio's release
docs.text:
Each file's effective detail is the same number duplicate detection uses to pick a keeper: the file's pixels, capped by what its bitrate can carry in its codec. A 1080p file at a starved bitrate counts as less than 1080p.

A file is compared with its peers: other scenes' files from the same studio.

  1. The same studio and the same year of release.
  2. If that group has fewer than 8 other files, the same studio within 2 years either side.
  3. If that still has fewer than 8, the whole studio.

The first group with at least 8 other files is used. A scene with no studio is never flagged, and neither is one whose studio has fewer than 8 other scenes.

A file is flagged only when both are true:

  • its effective detail is below the percentile of its peers' that you set (default 10th), and
  • it is under 0.6 times the peers' median.

The second test stops a studio whose files are all alike from flagging its own bottom 10%. The card shows the file's detail against the median, which peer group was used and how many peers it had, and the share of peers that are better.

docs.title: Blur and block sharpness
docs.text: For a below-studio file, Stash Sense also decodes six 3-second windows (at 10%, 25%, 40%, 55%, 70% and 85% of the file) and measures blur and blockiness with ffmpeg. The card shows the medians. Lower is better for both: a low blur number is a sharp picture, and a high block number means visible compression squares. These numbers are for you to judge. They do not decide the flag. They are cached per file.

docs.title: The percentile setting
docs.text: Peer percentile runs from 1 to 50 and defaults to 10. Raise it to see more cards, lower it to see fewer. The 0.6 times median test still applies at any value. Set it in Stash Sense > Settings > Curation > Quality flags.

docs.title: Tube or leak rips
docs.text:
Stage 1 looks only at clues in the file itself. Each clue has a weight, and the weights combine so that two weak clues can add up:

Clue Weight A well-known tube site in a container tag (title, comment, encoder and so on) 0.9 A tube site in the file name 0.6 Any other link or web address in a container tag 0.3 The file is below the studio's release (above) 0.2

The score is 1 - (1 - w1)(1 - w2).... A card is raised at 0.5 or more. A tube site in the name alone is enough, and a tube site in a tag is certainly enough. A stray link by itself (0.3) is not, and neither is a link together with low detail (0.44). The card lists each clue as signal: text.

docs.title: What waits for stage 2
docs.text:
Stage 1 never reads text off the picture. These wait for stage 2, which needs tesseract and more calibration:

  • an on-screen watermark that stays on for the whole video
  • a scrolling marquee along the bottom
  • a domain printed in the frames
  • pre-roll ads: a short clip at the start that is the same across many files. A trial run found that most hits were shared intro music, not ads, so stage 2 will confirm with shared video frames and count networks rather than single studios.

Until then, a rip with a clean file name and no tags is not flagged.

docs.title: Disfavored format
docs.text: A file whose video codec or container is on one of your disfavored lists raises the format flag, with the reason on the card. It shows only when nothing else is raised for the scene, so a broken or ripped file shows its more important problem first. With both lists empty the format flag never shows.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Run Quality Flags from Operations, or schedule it there. It runs weekly by default. The job:

  1. Reads the exclusion list. If Stash can't be reached, the run stops. Excluded scenes are skipped.
  2. Takes every scene's primary file and runs the cheap pass, then the deep check for suspects.
  3. Works out the peer groups and measures sharpness for below-studio files.
  4. Writes one recommendation per flagged scene, updating it in place on later runs.

A card you dismissed is not created again for the same scene. A card you answered stays answered while the scene keeps the same file, even when its peer evidence shifts; it comes back for review only when the file is replaced. A card whose file no longer has any flag, because you replaced the file or changed a setting, is resolved as stale on the next run. A card you have not answered is kept until then. The dashboard tile is Quality Flags. See Reviewing Recommendations for how cards work.

Quality cards are never high confidence and are not part of the batch accept. Every flag needs your own yes or no.

docs.title: Report-only and control cards
docs.text:
Report-only is on by default. While it is on, accepting a card only records your answers. It adds nothing to any group and changes nothing in Stash. The apply log keeps the entry. This is how you check the flags before you trust them.

While report-only is on, the job also keeps up to 20 control cards open. A control card is a random scene that had no flag, picked from scenes that never had a quality card. It looks like any other card but offers all four flags with the default no. Ask yourself whether anything is wrong with the file, and answer yes for what is.

docs.title: How your answers become calibration labels
docs.text:
Every accepted card stores your yes or no per flag. A dismissed card counts as no for every flag. scripts/quality_calibration.py reads them, and writes nothing:

python scripts/quality_calibration.py /path/to/stash_sense.db --unflagged 25000
  • Precision per flag: yes answers divided by reviewed flagged cards. Of the flags raised, how many were right.
  • Recall estimate per flag: from the control cards, the share of unflagged scenes you marked yes gives a miss rate. Combined with the number of unflagged scenes you pass in --unflagged, that estimates how many real problems the job did not flag, and so what share of all problems it did.

Use --json for the raw numbers. A few dozen answers per flag give a rough picture. Hundreds give a useful one.

docs.title: Work-queue groups
docs.text:
Once the flags are right, turn report-only off to have accepted cards act. Each flag has its own group ID in Stash Sense > Settings > Curation > Quality flags: broken, rip, below studio and format. Create the groups in Stash first and paste their IDs.

With report-only off, accepting a card adds the scene to the group of each flag you answered yes. A flag with no is left alone. A flag with no group set writes nothing, and a scene already in the group is not added again. The groups are your work queue: work through them with whatever tools you replace files with.

A flag answer other than yes or no is refused. If the scene is deleted, or its file is not the one the card was made for, the card can't be applied.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
All quality settings are stored in the stash-sense plugin's configuration in Stash, next to the curation settings.

Setting Default Meaning Report only on Accepting records answers and changes nothing. Broken, rip, below studio and format group IDs empty One Stash group per flag. Used only when report-only is off. Below-studio percentile 10 1 to 50. A file below this percentile of its peers, and under 0.6 times their median, is flagged.

docs.title: Reviewing Recommendations
docs.text: Curation features (duplicates, split points, metadata fixes) end with a decision only you should make. Stash Sense shows each one as a review card inside Stash. Nothing changes until you accept it, and every accepted change is logged.

docs.title: Opening the dashboard
docs.text: Click Stash Sense in Stash's top navigation bar, next to Scenes and Performers. It opens the dashboard at /plugins/stash-sense.

docs.title: The review card
docs.text:
Each card shows two things side by side:

  • Evidence: why the recommendation exists, such as the scene's files with size, codec, resolution and duration, stills taken from each file, and a Play here button that plays the scene from Stash's own stream at the relevant moment.
  • Outcome: exactly what accepting does:
    • each field that changes, with its value before and after
    • the files kept and the files deleted, by path and size
    • the space reclaimed

When a card offers choices (for example which file to keep, or an edited title), changing one rebuilds the outcome. The card always shows what Accept will do.

docs.title: Accepting
docs.text:
Accept applies the outcome shown on the card.

  • Deleting files needs a second confirm. The confirm lists every file by path and size. It also says where the files go: to Stash's trash folder if one is set (Settings > System > Trash path, Stash v0.30 and later), or permanently deleted if not.
  • If the library changed after the card loaded, for example someone edited the scene, accept is refused. Nothing is written, and the card reloads with the updated outcome for you to check again.
  • Accepting twice is harmless. A second accept of the same recommendation returns the first result and changes nothing.

docs.title: Accept all high-confidence
docs.text:
Each recommendation type marks the items it is confident about. Accept all high-confidence… on a type's page:

  1. lists how many items qualify, the field changes, every file that would be deleted and the total space reclaimed
  2. leaves every other item for individual review
  3. applies only after you confirm the summary

Batch accept always applies the type's suggestion. An item where you picked something different, such as another file to keep, is never batch-accepted. If any item in a batch is no longer high-confidence when it runs, the whole batch is refused and nothing is written.

docs.title: The apply log
docs.text:
Apply log on the dashboard lists every accepted change, newest first. Expand an entry to see the state before the change:

  • the old value of every field it changed
  • every deleted file's path, size and Stash fingerprints (oshash, md5, phash), and whether it went to the trash

Revert metadata writes the old field values back and reopens the recommendation. If a field was edited again after the apply, revert shows the edits and asks before it overwrites them. Revert cannot bring back deleted files; recover those from Stash's trash folder if one was set.

docs.title: Your corrections improve the suggestions
docs.text: When you accept something different from the suggestion, for example keeping another file or editing a proposed value, Stash Sense saves the suggestion, your choice and the evidence as a labeled example. These examples become the test set for that feature, so later versions are checked against your real decisions. The sidecar exports them at GET /review/labels?type=<type>.

docs.title: Unfinished types
docs.text: A recommendation type that has not passed the production checklist stays hidden. To see it, turn on Settings > Features > Show Unfinished Features. The Review Demo type is one of these: it only acts on scenes you tag stash-sense-review-demo, and it exists to try the review flow on a test library.

docs.title: Scene Tagger
docs.text: The Scene Stash-Box Tagger searches your untagged scenes across Stash-Box endpoints using file fingerprints to find matching metadata — title, studio, performers, tags, and more.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Perceptual hashes generated for scenes (Stash: Settings > Tasks > Generate > Perceptual Hashes)
  • At least one Stash-Box endpoint configured in Stash's Settings > Metadata Providers

File fingerprints (MD5, oshash, phash) are how Stash-Box endpoints identify your scenes. Without them, there's nothing to search with.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Trigger the Scene Stash-Box Tagger from the Operations tab or the recommendations dashboard
  2. Stash Sense queries each configured Stash-Box endpoint with your scenes' file fingerprints
  3. When a match is found, the upstream metadata is presented for review
  4. You can accept, modify, or skip each match before it's applied to your library

docs.title: What Gets Matched
docs.text:
When a scene's fingerprint matches on a Stash-Box endpoint, the following metadata is available:

  • Title and details
  • Date, director, and code
  • Studio assignment
  • Performer lineup with aliases
  • Tags
  • URLs

docs.title: UX Features
docs.text:
• Auto-expand search — Search results are automatically expanded when matches are found, reducing clicks
  • Local entity display — Matched performers and studios show whether they already exist in your local Stash library
  • Auto-matching with aliases — When a Stash-Box performer has aliases that match a local performer's name, the match is made automatically

docs.title: Running the Tagger
docs.text:
The tagger can be run from two places:

  • Operations tab — Trigger a full scan of unmatched scenes
  • Recommendations dashboard — Untagged scenes appear as recommendations; click to tag them

The tagger runs as a background job in the operation queue and supports incremental runs — only scenes modified or added since the last run are processed.

docs.title: Split Detection
docs.text:
Hidden as unfinished

Split detection is hidden until it passes the production-ready checklist (#131). To use it now, turn on Settings > Features > Show Unfinished Features and reload the page. Existing recommendations are kept and reappear when the setting is on.

Some files in a library hold more than one scene: a DVD rip with four scenes back to back, a compilation, a long file with a menu loop at the end. Stash Sense finds the boundaries inside these files and proposes where to cut. For each file you see a review card with the cut times, a before and an after still for every cut, and a button that plays the file from just before the cut. Nothing changes until you accept, and even then Stash Sense writes nothing to Stash. It hands the plan to stash-curator, which makes the cuts.

docs.title: What it scans
docs.text:
The job considers two kinds of scenes:

  • Scenes over 60 minutes.
  • Scenes whose file the Content Index shows holding another scene's whole file. A scene that was already split out, but whose source file is still in the library, is the usual case.

It skips:

  • scenes on the exclusion list (see Curation Settings)
  • the outputs of earlier splits, which are the scenes in the [curator] Split Cuts group and, for older runs, the scenes tagged [curator] split
  • a file whose plan you have already accepted. An accepted plan is never proposed again for the same file.

A title spread over several scenes (one title, several parts) is out of scope.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Run Split Multi-Scene Files from Operations, or schedule it there. It runs weekly by default and uses a lot of CPU. The job:

  1. Reads the exclusion list. If Stash can't be reached, the run stops.
  2. Finds the candidate scenes.
  3. Reads each file's signals, extracting them first if they are not cached.
  4. Plans every candidate and writes one recommendation per scene.

Then open the dashboard and look for the Split Multi-Scene Files tile. See Reviewing Recommendations for how cards work.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Each file is decoded once, in full, at 6 frames per second and 160 pixels wide, plus one pass over the audio. A 63-minute 360p test file took about 15 seconds. The signals are cached in splits.db in the data directory, keyed by the file's oshash and size, so a file is only decoded again if it changes or if a release changes what is extracted (the signals carry a version). Every run plans every candidate again from the cache, which is fast. When the planner improves, open plans are re-scored on the next run, and the job result says how many changed confidence or moved a cut by more than 2 seconds.

The job needs the media mount, like the other jobs that read files. See Configuration.

docs.title: How cuts are found
docs.text:
The planner works on the cached signals, not on the video again.

  • Blacks. A stretch of near-black frames, usually with silence or a sharp drop in volume, is a candidate boundary. Many productions put a fade to black between scenes. The cut goes at the start of the black. The black and any title card after it belong to the next scene.
  • Static pairs. Some sources separate scenes with a burst of static instead of a black. Pairs of these are treated as boundaries too.
  • Coverage. Where the Content Index shows that a stretch of the file is held by another scene's file, the edges of that stretch are cuts. An edge moves to the start of a nearby black run when there is one.
  • Menu tails. A DVD menu that loops at the end of a file is trimmed off, and the card shows it as keep until.
  • Series profiles. Scenes from one series tend to be cut the same way: how long the black lasts, whether there is a static burst, how long a scene runs. The planner learns this per series from cuts you have accepted before, and uses it to confirm good candidates and to drop odd ones.

Chapter markers and generic scene-change detection are not used. They did not find the boundaries reliably.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text:
Every card has a confidence. It decides whether the card can be taken in the batch accept.

Confidence What it means High The plan is confirmed by one of two things: a series profile where the scenes are mostly separated by blacks, or Content Index coverage of at least 90% of the file where a detected cut confirms every coverage edge. High plans can be accepted in a batch. Medium The planner found cuts and every resulting scene runs between 5 and 60 minutes. Look at the card before accepting. Low Anything else. A file with no cuts at all is suggested as leave whole.

There is no high confidence for a file just because it looks clear: without a profile or coverage to confirm it, a plan is at most medium. The planner is tested against a regression set of labelled titles. See the split regression for the numbers and what changed after the first run.

docs.title: Reviewing a card
docs.text:
Each card shows the file, its length, the confidence and the reasons behind it. Below that is one row per cut with its time, what kind of boundary it is, the evidence, a before and an after still, and a play from button that plays the file from five seconds before the cut. Blacks that were found but not used are listed as unconfirmed blacks. The Outcome panel lists the ranges that will be handed to stash-curator.

You can adjust the plan with three fields:

  • Cut times. The cut times as text, separated by commas. Use h:mm:ss, mm:ss or plain seconds, for example 22:40, 1:05:10. Empty with no trims means leave whole.
  • Keep from and Keep until. Trim the start or the end of the file, for example to drop a menu loop. Empty keeps the start or the end.

A time you type snaps to the start of a black run when one starts within 4 seconds before it to 2 seconds after it. This lets you type a rough time from a player and still cut where the scene starts. The Outcome panel says how many cuts snapped. A time with no black near it is used as typed. The Outcome panel updates to the new ranges as you preview.

docs.title: Leave whole
docs.text: A file with no cuts is suggested as leave whole. Accepting it records that decision and the plan is not proposed again for that file.

docs.title: Redundant files
docs.text: A file whose every stretch, outside its first and last seconds, is held by other scenes' files at equal or better quality gets a redundant card. It lists the covering scenes as links. Accepting only resolves the card. It deletes nothing and splits nothing. Deleting the redundant file belongs to duplicate detection.

docs.title: What accept does
docs.text: Accepting writes nothing to Stash. It marks the recommendation resolved and records the plan with it. Because nothing changed in Stash, a split-only accept can't be reverted from the apply log. The log keeps the entry for reference.

docs.title: Handing the plan to stash-curator
docs.text:
An accepted plan appears in the driver API at resolution.details.split:

{"scene_id": "7", "file_id": "70", "oshash": "abc", "size": 1000, "duration": 3000.0,
 "ranges": [{"start": 0.0, "end": 1500.0}, {"start": 1500.0, "end": 3000.0}],
 "cuts": [1500.0]}

ranges has one entry per scene to create, in seconds of the file. A leave-whole decision has split: null, and there is nothing to execute.

stash-curator reads accepted plans with split --from-sense (#111), cuts the file and creates the scenes. It then reports what it did with POST /api/v1/driver/recommendations/{id}/split-result. The result is stored with the recommendation and logged. See the driver API for the fields.

docs.title: Seeding series profiles
docs.text:
Profiles start empty and fill in as you accept plans. To start with more, place a split_seed.json file in the data directory. On the next run the job imports it once and renames it split_seed.json.imported. It holds labelled cuts for the series you have already split by hand. Build it with scripts/build_split_seed.py, which reads your existing labels and splits and writes the file. The seed names real series, so it is built locally and never belongs in a repository.

After the seed, every accepted plan with cuts adds a label on each run, and a re-run overwrites its own labels rather than adding duplicates.

docs.title: Upstream Changes
docs.text: Stash Sense detects metadata changes on Stash-Box endpoints and presents per-field merge controls to keep your local Stash library in sync. This covers performers, studios, and scenes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• At least one Stash-Box endpoint configured in Stash's Settings > Metadata Providers
  • Performers, studios, or scenes in your library linked to Stash-Box IDs

docs.title: 3-Way Diff Engine
docs.text:
For each field, the diff engine compares three states:

  • Upstream — Current value on the Stash-Box endpoint
  • Local — Current value in your Stash library
  • Snapshot — Last-seen upstream value (stored locally by Stash Sense)

This three-way comparison distinguishes intentional local differences from actual upstream changes. If you've deliberately set a different name locally, it won't keep suggesting the upstream name on every sync cycle.

docs.title: Change Detection
docs.text: A field is flagged only when the upstream value has changed since the last snapshot and the new upstream value differs from your local value. Fields where upstream hasn't changed, or where your local value already matches upstream, are skipped.

docs.title: Performer Sync
docs.text:
Detects field changes for performers linked to Stash-Box endpoints.

Per-field merge controls:

Field type Options Name fields Keep local / Accept upstream / Demote to alias / Add as alias / Custom Aliases Union checkboxes (pick which aliases to keep) Simple fields Keep local / Accept upstream / Custom

docs.title: Studio Sync
docs.text:
Detects changes for studios linked to Stash-Box endpoints.

Tracked fields:

  • Name — Studio display name
  • URL — Studio website
  • Parent studio — Hierarchical studio relationships (resolved via Stash-Box IDs, not name matching)

docs.title: Scene Sync
docs.text:
Detects metadata changes for scenes linked to Stash-Box endpoints.

Tracked field categories:

Category Fields Core metadata Title, details, date, director, code, URLs Studio assignment Studio linked to the scene Performer lineup Added/removed performers, alias changes Tags Tag set additions and removals

Performer lineup changes show which performers were added or removed upstream, including alias detection when an upstream performer's credited name differs from the local alias.

docs.title: Dismissal
docs.text:
When you review an upstream change and decide not to apply it:

  • Soft dismiss — Hides the recommendation for now. If the upstream value changes again in a future sync, the recommendation reappears.
  • Permanent dismiss — Skips this field/entity entirely in future syncs. Use this when your local value is intentionally different.

docs.title: Dismiss All
docs.text: The Dismiss All button lets you dismiss all currently visible upstream change recommendations at once. This is useful after reviewing a batch and deciding to skip the remaining items. Dismiss All applies a soft dismiss — if upstream changes again, items will reappear.

docs.title: Endpoint Enable/Disable Toggle
docs.text:
Each Stash-Box endpoint can be individually enabled or disabled for upstream sync analysis. Disabled endpoints are skipped during analysis runs but their configuration is preserved.

Use this to:

  • Temporarily pause sync from a noisy endpoint
  • Focus on changes from a single endpoint at a time
  • Disable endpoints you only use for scene tagging, not upstream sync

Toggle endpoints in the plugin's Settings tab under the Stash-Box Endpoints section.

docs.title: Merge Conflict Improvements
docs.text:
When the same field has been changed both locally and upstream since the last snapshot, an inline comparison panel shows:

  • The snapshot value (what the field was when last synced)
  • The local value (what you changed it to)
  • The upstream value (what Stash-Box changed it to)

This side-by-side view makes it easy to understand the conflict and decide which value to keep.

docs.title: Running Upstream Sync
docs.text:
Upstream analysis runs as a background job in the operation queue. It can be:

  • Triggered manually from the Operations tab
  • Scheduled to run automatically at a configurable interval
  • Run incrementally — only entities modified since the last watermark are checked, keeping sync fast after the initial scan

docs.title: Settings Page UI/UX Pass
docs.text: Date: 2026-02-19 Ticket: refactor: settings page UI/UX pass - consistent components, human-friendly intervals

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The plugin settings page has accumulated visual inconsistencies: - Job Schedules uses raw <input type="number"> with browser-native spinners and inline styles - Interval values displayed as raw hours (168 = 1 week) — meaningless at a glance - Three different coding patterns across Sidecar Settings, Job Schedules, and Upstream Sync sections - Inline styles scattered throughout stash-sense-settings.js instead of CSS classes - Inconsistent save patterns: auto-save vs explicit Save button

docs.title: Design Decisions
docs.text:
• Server-side interval definitions: JobDefinition gets allowed_intervals and description fields. The queue_types API serializes them to the frontend. Single source of truth.
  • Tiered interval presets: Light/Network jobs get frequent options (6h–2w), heavy/slow-changing jobs get infrequent options (1d–1mo).
  • Native <select> for interval picker: Styled to match dark theme. Accessible, zero JS overhead, options come from server.
  • Auto-save everywhere: All settings auto-save with 500ms debounce, except upstream field config (batch checkbox operation keeps explicit Save).
  • No new component abstractions: Use existing CSS classes consistently + add a few new ones. No UI library needed.
  • Defaults unchanged: 24h for DB update + upstream, 168h for duplicates + fingerprints.
